The meal that comes second in the day, after breakfast, is lunch.

In "The Sunflower," the author’s motive to explore the fragility of human connection and the inevitability of decay is structurally mirrored through the narrative arc of the sunflower itself. By aligning the protagonist’s internal state of isolation and sadness with the external, observable process of the sunflower wilting, the author creates a thematic parallel where the natural cycle of life and decay serves as a direct reflection of emotional neglect. This botanical metaphor is not merely decorative; it is central to the thematic structure, as the physical deterioration of the plant forces the reader to confront the same consequences of neglect that the protagonist faces in her personal relationships, thereby unifying the themes of nature and human emotion into a cohesive commentary on the impact of isolation.
